title: An AI-supported fragment-matching platform at LMU Munich identifies manuscripts that two scholars use to edit a lost Hymn to Babylon in the journal Iraq
summary: The AI-supported Electronic Babylonian Library platform at LMU Munich matched tablet fragments, which let two scholars edit a lost Hymn to Babylon from 21 manuscripts in 31 fragments.
account: Assyriologists Anmar A. Fadhil (University of Baghdad) and Enrique Jiménez (LMU Munich) edited a previously unknown Babylonian hymn that praises Babylon and its people. Their edition appeared online in the journal Iraq (volume 86) on 17 March 2025. The composition may have been about 250 lines long. It survives in no fewer than 20 manuscripts from the Sippar Library tablets, which date from the 7th to the 2nd/1st centuries BCE. The edition draws on the Electronic Babylonian Library (eBL), a fragment-matching platform that Jiménez's project at LMU Munich built. The article states that without the eBL platform the edition could not have used 21 manuscripts in 31 fragments. It credits the platform and its team and does not mention artificial intelligence. On 1 July 2025 LMU's press release said that the team's AI-supported platform had identified 30 further manuscripts belonging to the hymn. Jiménez said in the release that this process would formerly have taken decades. In December 2025 Archaeology Magazine, published by the Archaeological Institute of America, named the hymn one of its Top 10 Discoveries of 2025. Its writer reports that the team used AI models to search for overlaps and found 30 fragments from 20 tablets. On 24 September 2026 Shana Zaia of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam used the edited hymn in an Iraq article on religious education in Babylonian scribal schools.
purpose: Match and join cuneiform fragments across collections to reconstruct Babylonian literary texts
system: Electronic Babylonian Library (eBL) Fragmentarium, AI-supported fragment-matching platform
developer: LMU Munich, Institute of Assyriology (Enrique Jiménez's eBL project)
deployer: LMU Munich and University of Baghdad collaboration

ratings.reason: The teams at LMU Munich and the University of Baghdad published a peer-reviewed edition. The sources describe no change to either institution.

The edition recovers one lost literary text, which the LMU press release calls a fascinating hymn describing Babylon and its inhabitants. In 2026 a scholar who was not an author used the hymn as evidence for Babylonian scribal education.

ai_role.statement: The platform's matching identified additional manuscripts of the hymn (30 per the LMU release; the edition uses 21 manuscripts in 31 fragments per the article). The edition, translation and interpretation were done by the two authors. The AI attribution comes from the LMU release, in which Jiménez speaks of “our AI-supported platform”. The article credits the eBL platform and team without mentioning artificial intelligence. The LMU release is vendor-authored, since LMU is the platform's developer, and ScienceAlert mainly relays that release and the paper. The peer-reviewed edition appeared in Iraq. Its first author Anmar A. Fadhil is at the University of Baghdad, with one developer co-author (Jiménez).

Zaia works at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and is not an author of the edition; she thanks Aino Hätinen, a contributor to eBL editions, for comments. She uses the edited hymn as evidence for Babylonian scribal education, which shows that the recovered text has entered other scholarship, but she does not assess the platform's part in its recovery.

display.answer: The figures come from the makers' edition in Iraq and from LMU's press release of 1 July 2025, which ScienceAlert mainly relays along with the paper. Archaeology Magazine interviewed Jiménez, who gave new figures on fragment joins. Shana Zaia's 2026 study in Iraq uses the edited hymn and does not assess the platform's part in its recovery.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: The AI-supported Electronic Babylonian Library platform at LMU Munich matched tablet fragments, which let two scholars edit a lost Hymn to Babylon from 21 manuscripts in 31 fragments.
fields.account: Assyriologists Anmar A. Fadhil (University of Baghdad) and Enrique Jiménez (LMU Munich) edited a previously unknown Babylonian hymn that praises Babylon and its people. Their edition appeared online in the journal Iraq (volume 86) on 17 March 2025. The composition may have been about 250 lines long. It survives in no fewer than 20 manuscripts from the Sippar Library tablets, which date from the 7th to the 2nd/1st centuries BCE. The edition draws on the Electronic Babylonian Library (eBL), a fragment-matching platform that Jiménez's project at LMU Munich built. The article states that without the eBL platform the edition could not have used 21 manuscripts in 31 fragments. It credits the platform and its team and does not mention artificial intelligence. On 1 July 2025 LMU's press release said that the team's AI-supported platform had identified 30 further manuscripts belonging to the hymn. Jiménez said in the release that this process would formerly have taken decades. In December 2025 Archaeology Magazine, published by the Archaeological Institute of America, named the hymn one of its Top 10 Discoveries of 2025. Its writer reports that the team used AI models to search for overlaps and found 30 fragments from 20 tablets. On 24 September 2026 Shana Zaia of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam used the edited hymn in an Iraq article on religious education in Babylonian scribal schools.
